candidates.attacker_control: A remote, unauthenticated network client controls both required inputs: the HTTP Content-Type header (exact string application/x-java-serialized-object is attacker-set) and the request body bytes (a serialized Java object stream; a gzip Content-Encoding is also supported on the request path via HttpConverter/GZIPHelper). No credentials, route parameters, or application cooperation are needed beyond the deployment exposing a camel-http/camel-http4 consumer endpoint on a reachable port/path. On the client side, an attacker-controlled or compromised HTTP server (or a URL influenced via headers such as CamelHttpUri on a bridge endpoint) controls the response headers/body and thus the producer-side deserialization.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked for any disabling/opt-in control: global text search for allowJavaSerializedObject returns no matches, and the deserialization branch has no flag/size limit/filter. Checked whether other properties could suppress it: Exchange.DISABLE_HTTP_STREAM_CACHE and SKIP_GZIP_ENCODING/SKIP_WWW_FORM_URLENCODED do not gate the content-type branch. Checked whether the header filter strategy blocks the trigger: no, the branch reads request.getContentType() directly rather than the filtered header map (DefaultHttpBinding.java:138). Checked the default binding wiring: HttpEndpoint.getBinding() lazily instantiates DefaultHttpBinding, so no explicit configuration is needed for the vulnerable behaviour (HttpEndpoint.java:228-232). Checked reachability: the servlet is mounted at /* and dispatches to registered consumers (JettyHttpComponent.createServletForConnector lines 958-997), so any request to a camel-http consumer path triggers readRequest; the content type must match exactly, but the attacker chooses it. Checked the camel-http4 producer nuance: its extractResponseBody reads the content type from the HttpRequestBase rather than the HttpResponse (HttpProducer.java:306), which limits the client-side path there, so the claim relies primarily on the consumer paths and on camel-http's producer path (method.getResponseHeader). Not verified at runtime.
candidates.impact: With a gadget chain available, unauthenticated remote code execution in the Camel HTTP server (and equivalently in a Camel HTTP/AHC/Jetty/Netty-HTTP client consuming responses from an attacker-controlled server); otherwise attacker-triggerable deserialization of arbitrary object graphs leading to denial of service and, for weak configurations, information disclosure. Because deserialization occurs during HttpMessage construction, an application cannot mitigate it by requiring authentication/authorization inside the Camel route; it must replace the binding or upgrade to a version that gates this behaviour (no such gate exists in this snapshot).
candidates.prerequisites: 1) Application exposes a camel-http or camel-http4 consumer endpoint (e.g. from("http://0.0.0.0:8080/foo")) reachable by the attacker; 2) the default DefaultHttpBinding is used (explicit setBinding(...) replacement is non-default); 3) for code-execution impact, a usable gadget/deserialization chain must be present on the server classpath (Camel deployments typically bundle Spring/commons-collections/etc.); without a gadget the primitive still causes deserialization-side effects and typically denial of service (exception/throwable parsing attacker data, RuntimeCamelException propagation). The same conditions apply to the client-side variants when the peer HTTP server is attacker-influenced.
candidates.root_cause: The default HTTP binding deserializes the connection payload into a Java object based solely on a client-supplied Content-Type header. DefaultHttpBinding.readRequest() (camel-http and camel-http4) checks request.getContentType() against the literal application/x-java-serialized-object and then calls HttpHelper.deserializeJavaObjectFromStream(), which wraps the raw request bytes in java.io.ObjectInputStream and calls readObject() with no class allow-list, type filter, size/object-count limit, or opt-in flag. The check is performed while the HttpMessage is constructed (HttpMessage constructor -> HttpBinding.readRequest), i.e. inside the servlet before the exchange reaches any route or processor, so application/route-level validation, authentication or header filters cannot intervene. Camel-http's Jetty-based consumers register this servlet at /* (JettyHttpComponent.createServletForConnector) and CamelContinuationServlet extends the same CamelServlet, so every request to a camel-http consumer path reaches the vulnerable binding. The mirror-image producer/client code paths (response body with the same content type) are the same root cause. A global search for an allowJavaSerializedObject-style switch returns zero hits, confirming there is no built-in way to disable this behaviour in the snapshot.
candidates.title: Unauthenticated Java deserialization of HTTP request bodies in camel-http/camel-http4 (Content-Type: application/x-java-serialized-object)
candidates.trace: Incoming request -> org.apache.camel.component.http.CamelServlet.service() creates DefaultExchange and calls exchange.setIn(new HttpMessage(exchange, request, response)) (CamelServlet.java:118; identical in camel-http4/CamelServlet.java:75 and camel-jetty-common/CamelContinuationServlet.java:126, which extends this CamelServlet) -> HttpMessage constructor calls getEndpoint().getBinding().readRequest(request, this) (HttpMessage.java:52) -> DefaultHttpBinding.readRequest() forces body parsing, then if request.getContentType() equals application/x-java-serialized-object (DefaultHttpBinding.java:138 / http4:125) obtains an InputStream via mandatoryConvertTo(InputStream.class, body) and calls HttpHelper.deserializeJavaObjectFromStream(is) (line 141 / http4:128) -> HttpHelper creates new ObjectInputStream(is) (helper/HttpHelper.java:128 / http4 helper:112) and calls readObject() (line 130 / http4:114). This executes object graph deserialization before consumer.getProcessor().process(exchange) (CamelServlet.java:144), so route-level guards never see the request first. The client-side mirror: HttpProducer.extractResponseBody() returns HttpHelper.deserializeJavaObjectFromStream(response) when the response (camel-http) / request-side content type (camel-http4) matches (HttpProducer.java:296-297 / http4:314-315); DefaultAhcBinding.java:227-228, DefaultJettyHttpBinding.java:172-175 and NettyHttpHelper.java:141-146 apply the same content-type-gated readObject to remote responses. The P1 index corroborates the readRequest -> HttpHelper.deserializeJavaObjectFromStream call edge (components/camel-http/.../DefaultHttpBinding.java:141).
candidates.unverified: No code was executed and no exploit payload was built; RCE depends on an available gadget chain on the deployment classpath (not determinable from source), so the guaranteed effect of the primitive is arbitrary-object deserialization/DoS. The candidate is one unconfirmed lead, not a runtime-confirmed vulnerability. The exact upstream fix commit/CVE mapping was not verified from the snapshot (no VCS metadata or CVE references are present in the tree), and the P1 index provides no data-flow proof, so the trace is established by reading call sites in source.

coverage_summary: Coverage is partial and pattern-directed, not a full per-file audit of the 16,655 visible files (1 file withheld by the sensitive-name filter; 16,656 source-root files per the source scope tool). I ran repository-wide text searches for java.io.ObjectInputStream/ObjectInput and deserialization helper names, content-type constants, XML parser hardening (DocumentBuilderFactory/disallow-doctype-decl), command execution (ProcessBuilder/Runtime.exec) and script engines (ScriptEngineManager), then read the relevant call chains in camel-http, camel-http4, camel-ahc, camel-jetty-common, camel-netty-http, camel-shiro, camel-core XmlConverter and the servlet/endpoint wiring. The P1 relation index was used only for navigation (symbol/edge lookups on DefaultHttpBinding and HttpHelper.deserializeJavaObjectFromStream); it is explicitly partial: ~1,018 omitted files, 37 parse errors, 252,801 unresolved calls, and no control-flow, data-flow or semantic resolution, so it proves nothing about reachability and no claim here rests on an index label alone. The remaining ~16,000 files (most component implementations and tests) were not individually inspected.
limitations: No code was compiled, executed, deployed or fuzzed; findings are source-only and the submitted candidate is an unconfirmed lead, not a runtime-confirmed vulnerability.
No VCS metadata, fix commits, patches or benchmark metadata are present in the snapshot, so the relationship of this code to any specific upstream fix/advisory could not be verified.

The P1 index has no data-flow/control-flow analysis and reports incomplete coverage (omitted files, parse errors, unresolved calls); reachability was established by reading source call sites, not by the index.

Whether a usable deserialization gadget chain exists on any given deployment classpath cannot be determined from this repository; the guaranteed effect of the primitive is attacker-triggered deserialization (DoS/side effects), with RCE conditional on classpath gadgets.

Only a small fraction of the monorepo's components were inspected; other unexamined modules may contain additional issues, and the single candidate was chosen for the strongest evidence/impact among those actually reviewed.

No runtime authentication/authorization configuration of hypothetical deployments was available; the unauthenticated claim rests on the component having no built-in content-type guard and on the call happening before route processing.

rejected_leads.lead: camel-shiro ShiroSecurityProcessor deserializes the Shiro token with ObjectInputStream (components/camel-shiro/.../ShiroSecurityProcessor.java:117-126)
rejected_leads.reason: The token must first be decrypted with the passphrase configured on the endpoint/policy; a remote attacker without that key cannot produce a ciphertext that survives decryption into an attacker-chosen object stream, so this is not attacker-reachable by default.

rejected_leads.lead: camel-core XmlConverter XML parsing (XmlConverter.createDocumentBuilderFactory, camel-core/.../converter/jaxp/XmlConverter.java:1099-1126) does not set disallow-doctype-decl
rejected_leads.reason: It does disable external-general-entities (line 1106), sets a Xerces SecurityManager when available (1113-1118) and uses FEATURE_SECURE_PROCESSING for the TransformerFactory (1155); exposure also requires a route that converts untrusted XML to DOM. Partial hardening, weaker than the selected candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: Aggregation-repository deserialization of stored blobs (camel-sql JdbcCamelCodec/ClassLoadingAwareObjectInputStream, camel-cassandraql CassandraCamelCodec:78-81, camel-hbase HBaseHelper:84-96, camel-krati KratiDefaultSerializer:71-84)
rejected_leads.reason: These read Java objects from the aggregation repository (database/KV store). Exploitation requires a separate ability to write attacker-controlled blobs into that store (an additional trust boundary), and the code is only on the aggregation path; unverified.

rejected_leads.lead: Network-buffer converters expose ObjectInput over raw buffers (camel-mina MinaConverter.toObjectInput:65-67, camel-mina2 Mina2Converter:61-63, camel-netty NettyConverter:70-73, camel-netty4 NettyConverter:76-79, camel-hbase/camel-sql helpers)
rejected_leads.reason: These only wrap the data in an ObjectInputStream; readObject() happens only if route-specific code explicitly converts the body to ObjectInput, so it is not an automatic network-triggered deserialization and is route-dependent.

rejected_leads.lead: Client-side response deserialization in camel-http HttpProducer, camel-http4 HttpProducer, camel-ahc DefaultAhcBinding, camel-jetty-common DefaultJettyHttpBinding and camel-netty-http/netty4-http NettyHttpHelper (seralized-exception handling)
rejected_leads.reason: Same root cause as the selected candidate (content-type-gated readObject on remote bytes) and therefore not reported as separate candidates; additionally camel-http4's variant keys off the request's content type rather than the response's (HttpProducer.java:306), making that particular site less clearly attacker-triggerable.

rejected_leads.lead: camel-castor CastorDataFormat / other data-format unmarshalling of untrusted payloads
rejected_leads.reason: Requires a route that explicitly unmarshals untrusted data with that data format and depends on the third-party library's behaviour; not traced to a concrete remote-triggerable path in this snapshot and not verified.

summary: Snapshot is an Apache Camel 2.15-SNAPSHOT monorepo (16,655 model-visible files; one file withheld by the sensitive-name filter; P1 index reports 11,937 Java files, 1,018 omitted files, 37 parse errors, no control/data-flow or semantic resolution). Review was pattern-driven (ObjectInputStream/ObjectInput, deserialization helpers, DocumentBuilderFactory/XXE hardening, ProcessBuilder/Runtime.exec, ScriptEngineManager) plus targeted source reading of the HTTP consumers/producers and their entry points. The single strongest source-evidenced issue is content-type-gated Java native deserialization in camel-http/camel-http4: for any request handled by the Camel HTTP servlet the default binding deserializes the raw request body with ObjectInputStream whenever the attacker-supplied Content-Type header equals "application/x-java-serialized-object", and this happens while the HttpMessage is constructed, before any route/processor (and any route-level security logic) can run. No opt-in/opt-out guard exists anywhere in the tree. The same unguarded pattern exists in the HTTP clients/producers (camel-http, camel-http4, camel-ahc, camel-jetty-common, camel-netty-http/netty4-http), i.e. one root cause with several call sites; it is reported as one candidate. Other deserialization/XXE leads were examined and rejected as weaker or requiring additional trust boundaries (see rejected_leads).
